newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Former Albanian leader Ramiz Alia still on the run.
newsitem.headline: Former Albanian leader Ramiz Alia still on the run.

text.p: Albania's last communist leader, Ramiz Alia, who fled from jail last month with hundreds of other prisoners is still on the run, the Justice Ministry said on Tuesday.
Albanian newspapers on Tuesday reported that Alia had fled the country and was in France, where he was with son, Arben.

"Alia has not returned voluntarily to jail so far, and we really don't know where he is," Justice Ministry spokesman Agim Neza said of the handpicked successor to dictator Enver Hoxha who led Albania between 1985 and 1992.

Alia, 72, and other former communist senior officials were among 1,309 inmates who escaped from Albania's seven jails when their guards fled during an armed uprising swept Europe's poorest country in March.
Alia was arrested last year and charged with crimes against humanity. He was awaiting trial when he fled jail last month. If convicted, he would face a sentence of 15 years to death.
Prosecutors started investigating Alia after parliament passed a law in 1995 which banned former communist officials from holding public office until 2002.

Three senior ex-communists were sentenced to death in May, charged with crimes against humanity for ordering the deportation of anti-communist dissidents. An appeals court revoked the sentences and imposed lengthy jail terms instead.
More than 30 ex-communists were sentenced to up to 25 years in jail for crimes against humanity.

Around 100,000 Albanians are thought to have been forced into internal exile in remote villages during the 45 years of communist rule because of opposition to the Stalinist government or for trying to escape from the isolated Balkan country.

But Alia, president until March 1992 when President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party won a landslide victory in general elections, has the denied allegations and said his arrest was politically motivated.
"It is clear I am a political prisoner and being tried as an opponent of the current regime," he wrote in a newspaper commentary early this year.

Neza said about 700 of the 1,309 escaped prisoners would not have to spend any more time behind bars because of an amnesty offered to all those who returned voluntarily. Those who returned before April 12 had their sentences cut by one-third.
"So far, only 67 out of 600 people who left the jails had returned on their own free will" Neza said.
